inbox.content: Polar bears (Ursus maritimus) depend on sea ice as a platform for hunting seals. Arctic sea ice has declined in extent and thickness over the satellite era as the Arctic has warmed about twice as fast as the global mean (Arctic amplification). The IUCN and Arctic scientists treat loss of sea-ice hunting habitat as the primary long-term threat to the species. Some subpopulations have been relatively stable or better counted in recent surveys, which deniers sometimes quote as 'polar bears are fine.' That snapshot does not cancel the physical dependence on ice or projections of increased fasting and reduced cub survival as ice-free seasons lengthen, especially in southern parts of the range. Polar-bear numbers are not a single global census with low error; management units differ. Conservation hunting quotas and pollution are additional pressures, but they do not make sea-ice loss irrelevant. There is no scientific basis for the claim that polar bears are thriving because of chemtrails or that global warming is a hoax because one subpopulation increased.

history.contentIn: The Stratospheric Controlled Perturbation Experiment (SCoPEx) was a Harvard University scientific proposal to study how tiny amounts of aerosol particles behave in the stratosphere. Principal investigator Frank Keutsch and collaborators including David Keith described the concept publicly, including at the American Geophysical Union Fall Meeting in 2017. The experiment was designed to improve computer models used to estimate risks and benefits of solar geoengineering (solar radiation management). It was not a test of deploying geoengineering and was not intended to cool the planet. The planned platform was a scientific balloon gondola with propellers, flying near 20 km altitude. A very small amount of material — on the order of 100 grams to less than 2 kilograms, typically calcium carbonate (a common mineral found in limestone and used in products such as toothpaste) — would be released into a small mixed volume roughly 1 km long and 100 meters in diameter. The gondola would then fly back through that plume to measure aerosol microphysics, chemistry, and light scattering. A 2021 platform test in Sweden, planned with the Swedish Space Corporation from Esrange, was a hardware test only: the SCoPEx Advisory Committee recommended suspending it pending societal engagement, and no particles were to be released. In March 2024 Harvard announced that Keutsch was no longer pursuing SCoPEx; the platform is expected to be repurposed for stratospheric research unrelated to solar geoengineering.

history.contentIn: Stratospheric aerosol injection (SAI) is a proposed solar radiation modification method that would introduce aerosols into the stratosphere to reflect a small fraction of incoming sunlight, analogous in mechanism to cooling after large volcanic eruptions such as Mount Pinatubo in 1991. The IPCC has described SAI as the most-researched solar geoengineering approach and notes that, used at moderate intensity, it could limit warming, but imperfectly and with other possible effects if used suboptimally. Candidate materials discussed in the literature include sulfates and, in some proposals, calcite or other particles. Delivery concepts include specialised high-altitude aircraft; there is no operational global SAI deployment. SAI would not remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, would not stop ocean acidification, and would require a sustained commitment if used to offset continued high emissions. Risks discussed in assessments include ozone chemistry, changes in precipitation patterns, termination shock if a program stopped abruptly, and governance problems. Small research proposals such as Harvard's SCoPEx aimed to measure aerosol microphysics in a tiny plume, not to cool the planet. Public claims that routine commercial aviation is already injecting SAI materials as 'chemtrails' are not supported by atmospheric science.

Candidate materials discussed in the literature include sulfates and, in some proposals, calcite or other particles. Delivery concepts include specialised high-altitude aircraft; there is no operational global SAI deployment. SAI would not remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, would not stop ocean acidification, and would require a sustained commitment if used to offset continued high emissions. Risks discussed in assessments include ozone chemistry, changes in precipitation patterns, termination shock if a program stopped abruptly, and governance problems. Small research proposals such as Harvard's SCoPEx aimed to measure aerosol microphysics in a tiny plume, not to cool the planet. Public claims that routine commercial aviation is already injecting SAI materials as 'chemtrails' are not supported by atmospheric science.

The Paris Agreement is a legally binding international treaty on climate change adopted by 196 Parties at COP21 in Paris on 12 December 2015 and in force from 4 November 2016. Its central aim is to hold the increase in the global average temperature to well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels and to pursue efforts to limit the increase to 1.5°C. Parties submit nationally determined contributions (NDCs) describing their mitigation plans; the Agreement uses a ratchet mechanism of successive NDCs rather than a single top-down allocation of tonnes. The treaty does not ban talking about geoengineering, but it is not a secret authorisation to spray the atmosphere. Article 4 addresses peaking of greenhouse gas emissions and a balance between anthropogenic emissions by sources and removals by sinks in the second half of the century (often discussed as net-zero CO2). The United States joined, withdrew under the first Trump administration, and rejoined under the Biden administration; participation has been politically contested but the scientific case for rapid emissions cuts is independent of any one administration. Meeting Paris temperature goals requires deep, sustained cuts in fossil CO2, methane and other greenhouse gases, plus protection of carbon sinks — not covert aviation spraying.

history.contentIn: The scientific consensus regarding the reality of recent global warming, primarily driven by human greenhouse gas emissions, is well-documented in Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) assessment reports and numerous literature surveys. Studies by Cook et al. (2013, 2016) indicate that approximately 97% of peer-reviewed papers that take a stance support the notion of anthropogenic global warming, with later surveys of climate scientists showing similar levels of agreement. Polar bears (Ursus maritimus) depend on sea ice as a platform for hunting seals. Arctic sea ice has declined in extent and thickness over the satellite era as the Arctic has warmed about twice as fast as the global mean (Arctic amplification). The IUCN and Arctic scientists treat loss of sea-ice hunting habitat as the primary long-term threat to the species. Some subpopulations have been relatively stable or better counted in recent surveys, which deniers sometimes quote as 'polar bears are fine.' That snapshot does not cancel the physical dependence on ice or projections of increased fasting and reduced cub survival as ice-free seasons lengthen, especially in southern parts of the range. Polar-bear numbers are not a single global census with low error; management units differ. Conservation hunting quotas and pollution are additional pressures, but they do not make sea-ice loss irrelevant. There is no scientific basis for the claim that polar bears are thriving because of chemtrails or that global warming is a hoax because one subpopulation increased.
